description: We’re Klashka, a team combining software, AI, and wearable technology to bring astronaut health and radiation data into one clear picture. Our mission is to help protect the people pushing humanity farther into space.
summary:
We developed Kha-device 01 , an astronaut-monitoring prototype that combines physiological data and radiation-exposure readings in one platform. Its proposed wearable harness integrates a vital-signs unit and an active dosimeter. The current software uses simulated readings to demonstrate secure data collection, storage, visualization, and comparisons against each person’s baseline.

The project addresses the challenge of understanding astronaut health alongside environmental conditions. Its dashboard brings together heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and dosimetry, with optional NASA space-weather context. A three-stage summary system organizes physiological findings, space-related information, and a combined overview, using rule-based summaries or optional local AI models.

This matters because crews need clear, trustworthy information, especially when assistance from Earth is delayed. By highlighting changes and missing data while preserving measurement history, Kha device 01 provides a foundation for future monitoring and decision-support research. The prototype remains simulation-based and requires hardware integration and clinical and flight validation before operational use.
details:
Kha-device 01 is an astronaut-monitoring prototype that brings physiological measurements and radiation-exposure data into one platform. Our concept combines two devices on a wearable harness: a vital-signs unit and an active ionizing-radiation dosimeter. By presenting both data streams together, the project aims to give astronauts and mission teams a clearer understanding of changes during a mission.

The current prototype demonstrates this workflow using simulated heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and dosimeter readings. Python simulators send timestamped JSON packets through an authenticated API. The backend validates and stores these readings, prevents duplicate records when transmissions are repeated, and displays their history in a dashboard. Its statistical analysis compares recent physiological readings with the same person’s earlier baseline, identifies changes in dosimeter counters, and highlights missing or unreliable data. An optional connection to NASA’s DONKI API adds radiation-belt event information as environmental context, kept separate from personal dose measurements.

The project also includes a three-stage summary system: a health specialist, a space specialist, and a synthesis stage that combines their findings. The language-model configuration uses a medically fine-tuned Llama 3.2 3B model, an astronomy LoRA adapter applied to Llama 3.2 3B, and IBM Granite 3.3 2B for synthesis. These models can run locally through Ollama; a Hugging Face Transformers and PEFT backend is also implemented. The hosted demonstration currently uses rule-based summaries. Numerical findings are calculated directly from the readings, while model-generated text is checked for unsupported figures.

The main intended benefit is to reduce the effort required to review separate physiological and radiation records. Personal baseline comparisons help make individual changes visible, while combined summaries organize findings, uncertainties, and missing information. Our longer-term goal is to support better-informed crew monitoring and future decision-support research, particularly for missions where assistance from Earth may be delayed. Simulators also make the software accessible for testing and demonstration before physical instruments are available.

We developed the backend with Python, Django, Django REST Framework, and PostgreSQL, with SQLite available for local development. The dashboard uses Django templates, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The bilingual public website uses Astro, TypeScript, and Three.js to explain the system through interactive 3D visuals. Development tools include GitHub, uv, Bun, Ruff, and automated tests, with deployment on Railway. Proposed hardware includes MAX86178 and MAX30205 components for physiological sensing, two DIS radiation-detection chambers, an STM32 microcontroller, FRAM storage, a TMP117 temperature sensor, and an RV-3028 clock. These components inform the design and simulated profiles; physical integration remains future work.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting wearable physiology, personal dosimetry, environmental context, and specialized text generation within one workflow. Our team considered spaceflight challenges such as radiation, altered gravity, isolation, and distance from Earth, alongside practical engineering concerns: privacy, interrupted communications, data integrity, computational limits, and AI-generated errors. These considerations shaped features such as individual device credentials, retry-safe ingestion, preserved timestamps and units, and explicit separation of simulated and hardware data. Kha-device 01 currently demonstrates data collection, comparison, and summarization; clinical and flight validation remain necessary before operational use.
